title: CHAPTER TWO. On the grace of redemption; incarnation and the person of Christ
latin: CAPUT SECUNDUM, De gratia redemtionis: ubi de incarnatione & persona Christi. HActenus de gratia paternae miserationis: sequitur gratia fraternae redemtionis, quae est alterum salutis nostrae principium, quo Filius Dei, tanquam mediator philanthropus, humanum genus lapsum, salva iustitia, Patri suo secundum ordinem & promissionem novae gratiae reconciliavit. Nam gratia miserationis, quam capite praecedenti explicavimus, ita comparata est, ut divinae iustitiae, qua peccatum odit & punit, partes suae nihilominus integrae maneant, neque ei per misericordiam Dei quicquam derogetur. Cui ut satisfaceret, oportuit ipsum Dei Filium humanam naturam induere, ut homo pro hominibus satisfaceret & Deus ita huic satisfactioni infinitam quandam vim infereret. Nam infinitae iustitiae a nobis laesae non nisi per obedientiam & passionem aliquo modo infinitam satisfieri potuit. Ingens haec gratia est, teste Davide Psal. 49:8-9. II. Sunt autem hic consideranda personae Christi incarnatio, officium, status & satisfactio.
english: CHAPTER TWO. On the grace of redemption: where of the incarnation and person of Christ.

Thus far concerning the grace of paternal mercy: there follows the grace of fraternal redemption, which is the second principle of our salvation, by which the Son of God, as philanthropic mediator, reconciled the fallen human race to His Father, justice being kept safe, according to the order and promise of the new grace.

For the grace of mercy explained in the preceding chapter is so arranged that the parts of divine justice, by which He hates and punishes sin, nevertheless remain whole, and nothing is derogated from it by Gods mercy. That this might be satisfied, it was necessary that the Son of God Himself put on human nature, so that a human might satisfy for humans and God might thus put a certain infinite force into this satisfaction. For infinite justice injured by us could be satisfied only by an obedience and passion in some way infinite. This grace is immense, as David testifies in Psalm 49:8-9.
II. Here are to be considered the incarnation, office, state, and satisfaction of the person of Christ.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Here stand as to be considered ye incarnation, office, state, and satisfaction belonging toward ye person belonging toward Christ. — II. — This grace stands as immense, as David testifies in Psalm 49:8-9. — For infinite justice injured by us could be satisfied only by an obedience and passion in some way infinite. — That this might be satisfied, it was necessary that ye Son belonging toward God Himself put on human nature, so that a human might satisfy toward humans and God might thus put a certain infinite force into this satisfaction. — For ye grace belonging toward mercy explained in ye preceding chapter stands as so arranged that ye parts belonging toward divine justice, by which He hates and punishes sin, nevertheless remain whole, and nothing stands as derogated out from it by Gods mercy. — there follows ye grace belonging toward fraternal redemption, which stands as ye second principle belonging toward our salvation, by which ye Son belonging toward God, as philanthropic mediator, reconciled ye fallen human race to His Father, justice being kept safe, according to ye order and promise belonging toward ye new grace. — Thus far concerning ye grace belonging toward paternal mercy: — where belonging toward ye incarnation and person belonging toward Christ. — On ye grace belonging toward redemption: — CHAPTER TWO.

title: III. Incarnation defined; personal subsistence communicated to the assumed nature
latin: III. Incarnatio est, qua aeternus Dei Filius, natura humana in unitatem personae assumpta, definito tempore e muliere homo factus est, ut inter Deum & homines mediatorem ageret. Huius fundamenta exhibent Psal. 45:8; Esa. 7:14; 1 Pet. 1:20; Ioh. 1:14; Matth. 1:21 & 16:16; Gal. 4:4; 1 Ioh. 4:2; 1 Tim. 2:5; Hebr. 2:14. De hac gratia Apostolus 1 Tim. 3:16 asserit, quod sit magnum pietatis mysterium. Haec autem incarnatio ita facta est, quantum e scripturis discimus, ut superveniente in beatam virginem Mariam Spiritu sancto, & inumbrante eam virtute altissimi, ipsa conceperit atque pepererit Filium Dei, naturam videlicet humanam, individuam & singularem, quam sine virili semine, per omnipotentem virtutem ipsi Filio cum Patre & Spiritu sancto communem, virgo conceperat, Filius in unitatem personae assumpsit, sive, quod idem pollet, personaliter sibi univit & naturae illi humanae communicavit terminum & gradum ultimum substantialem, quo natura intelligens in genere substantiae completur. Cum enim persona sit rationalis natura incommunicabilis substantia, personalitatem nos dicimus id ipsum quo persona constituitur in esse personali ultimo & completo, & quo incommunicabilis efficitur. Talem personalitatem natura ex virgine concepta ex sese habere potuisset; at ne duae personae essent, sed una, idcirco Filius Dei suam propriam ei communicavit & assumptam naturam sua prima & intima perfectione personali terminavit, substantialiter complevit, atque in esse ultimo hypostatico & incommunicabili constituit.
english: III. Incarnation is that by which the eternal Son of God, human nature having been assumed into the unity of person, at a definite time was made human from a woman, that He might act as mediator between God and humans. Its foundations are shown in Psalm 45:8; Isaiah 7:14; 1 Peter 1:20; John 1:14; Matthew 1:21 and 16:16; Galatians 4:4; 1 John 4:2; 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 2:14. Of this grace the Apostle asserts in 1 Timothy 3:16 that it is the great mystery of godliness.

This incarnation, as we learn from the Scriptures, took place thus: the Holy Spirit coming upon the blessed virgin Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowing her, she conceived and bore the Son of God — that is, an individual and singular human nature, which without male seed, by the omnipotent power common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the virgin had conceived, and which the Son assumed into the unity of person, or, what amounts to the same, personally united to Himself and communicated to that human nature the ultimate substantial term and degree by which an intelligent nature is completed in the genus of substance.

For since a person is a rational nature as incommunicable substance, we call personality that very thing by which a person is constituted in the ultimate and complete personal being, and by which it is made incommunicable. Such personality the nature conceived from the virgin could have had of itself; but lest there be two persons rather than one, the Son of God therefore communicated His own to it and terminated the assumed nature by His first and intimate personal perfection, completed it substantially, and constituted it in the ultimate hypostatic and incommunicable being.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Of this grace ye Apostle asserts in 1 Timothy 3:16 that it stands as ye great mystery belonging toward godliness. — Hebrews 2:14. — 1 Timothy 2:5; — 1 John 4:2; — Galatians 4:4; — Matthew 1:21 and 16:16; — John 1:14; — 1 Peter 1:20; — Isaiah 7:14; — Its foundations stand as shown in Psalm 45:8; — Incarnation stands as that by which ye eternal Son belonging toward God, human nature having been assumed into ye unity belonging toward person, at a definite time was made human out from a woman, that He might act as mediator between God and humans. — III.

title: IV–VI. Truth of the two natures in the incarnate person; divine and human
latin: IV. In persona Christi incarnata spectantur duarum naturarum, divinae & humanae, veritas, earumque personalis unio. V. Divina natura in Christo est, qua ipse Filius Dei aeternus humanam naturam sibi personaliter univit. Natura divina, ut recte docent Theol. Leidenses synops. disp. XXV th. 9, non hic proprie intelligitur incarnata, qua tribus personis communis est, sed qua Filii est, singulari modo subsistendi distincta. Non quod alia atque alia sit Deitas Patris & Spiritus S., sed quod Verbum essentiae in Filio distincte consideretur, tanquam ipsi a Patre per aeternam generationem communicata, 1 Tim. 3:16; Col. 2:9; Prov. 8:22-23; Ioh. 1:1,14 & 8:58; Phil. 2:6 — id quod adversus Photinianos, Arianos, Servetistas & Socinistas orthodoxi Theologi solidissime demonstrant. VI. Humana natura in Christo est, quae ab eo omnibus partibus & proprietatibus essentialibus suis absoluta ex carne Mariae virginis in unitatem personae assumpta est. Ab hac natura Filius Dei dicitur caro factus Ioh. 1:14 per synecdochen, quippe integer homo corpore vero & anima rationali constans, & quidem non exclusa humili ac misera hominum conditione simul & origine, Phil. 2:7; Ioh. 1:14; 2 Cor. 8:9; Heb. 2:14 & 4:15. Unde & genealogia ipsius ad Adamum ducitur, Luc. 3:38, adversus Marcionem & Manichaeos, corpus Christi non nisi apparens & simulatum fingentes, & Valentinianos negantes Christum carnem suam e substantia virginis matris assumpsisse. Quia verus homo est, habebit quae hominis essentiam constituunt & sine quibus hominem esse contradictionem involveret; nimirum corpus animatum & animam rationalem, intellectu & voluntate praeditam.
english: IV. In the incarnate person of Christ are contemplated the truth of the two natures, divine and human, and their personal union.

V. The divine nature in Christ is that by which He Himself, the eternal Son of God, personally united human nature to Himself. The divine nature, as the Leiden theologians rightly teach (Synopsis, disputation XXV, thesis 9), is not here properly understood as incarnate insofar as it is common to the three persons, but insofar as it is the Sons, distinct by a singular mode of subsistence — not as if the Deity of the Father and of the Holy Spirit were other and other, but because the Word of the essence is distinctly considered in the Son as communicated to Him from the Father by eternal generation (1 Timothy 3:16; Colossians 2:9; Proverbs 8:22-23; John 1:1,14; 8:58; Philippians 2:6). Orthodox theologians demonstrate this most solidly against Photinians, Arians, Servetists, and Socinians.

VI. The human nature in Christ is that which, absolute in all its essential parts and properties, was assumed by Him from the flesh of the virgin Mary into the unity of person. From this nature the Son of God is called made flesh (John 1:14) by synecdoche, as a whole human consisting of a true body and a rational soul — and indeed not excluding the humble and miserable condition and origin of humans (Philippians 2:7; John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Hebrews 2:14; 4:15). Hence His genealogy is also led to Adam (Luke 3:38), against Marcion and the Manichees who invent Christs body as only apparent and simulated, and against the Valentinians who deny that Christ assumed His flesh from the substance of the virgin mother. Because He is a true human, He will have what constitutes a humans essence and without which to be human would involve a contradiction: namely an animated body and a rational soul endowed with intellect and will.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): VI. — Orthodox theologians demonstrate this most solidly against Photinians, Arians, Servetists, and Socinians. — Philippians 2:6). — 8:58; — John 1:1,14; — Proverbs 8:22-23; — Colossians 2:9; — The divine nature, as ye Leiden theologians rightly teach (Synopsis, disputation XXV, thesis 9), stands as not here properly understood as incarnate insofar as it stands as common to ye three persons, but insofar as it stands as ye Sons, distinct by a singular mode belonging toward subsistence — not as if ye Deity belonging toward ye Father and belonging toward ye Holy Spirit were other and other, but because ye Word belonging toward ye essence stands as distinctly considered in ye Son as communicated to Him out from ye Father by eternal generation (1 Timothy 3:16; — The divine nature in Christ stands as that by which He Himself, ye eternal Son belonging toward God, personally united human nature to Himself. — V. — In ye incarnate person belonging toward Christ stand as contemplated ye truth belonging toward ye two natures, divine and human, and their personal union. — IV.

title: VII–X. Conception, assumption, and nativity of the human nature
latin: VII. Humanae naturae porro consideratur conceptio, assumptio & nativitas. VIII. Conceptio est, qua, singulari quadam Spiritus S. operatione, ea in utero Mariae virginis ex eiusdem semine exsistere coepit. Id docetur Gen. 3:15; Esa. 7:14; Matth. 1:18,20; Luc. 1:30-31 — & quidem supernaturaliter & immediata Spiritus S. virtute, cuius respectu singulariter non genitus, sed factus dicitur Rom. 1:3; Gal. 4:4; & sancte, Luc. 1:34-35; Heb. 7:26; & comparatur cum primo Adamo, non quod ad corporis materiam, sed quod ad conceptionis modum, Rom. 5:14; 1 Cor. 15:45,47. IX. Assumptio humanae naturae a Verbo est, qua Filius Dei substantiam illam humanam in utero Mariae, proprie subsistentiae sive personalitatis expertem, primo statim conceptionis momento, suam personalitatem largitus est. Nam recte Leo Magnus ep. XI: Natura, inquit, nostra non sic assumpta est, ut prius creata post assumeretur, sed ut ipsa assumptione crearetur. Ne quis forte existimet humanitatem exstitisse antequam Verbo uniretur. Confer Heb. 2:16; Col. 2:9; Phil. 2:7. X. Nativitas est, qua Filius Dei a Maria virgine maturo & legitimo pariendi tempore verus homo in lucem editus est. Ex praedictione Mosis Gen. 49:10 & Esaiae 7:14; Mich. 5:2; Lucas 2:6-7,22-23 natalia Christi docet, ut & Paulus Gal. 4:4.
english: VII. Further, of the human nature are considered conception, assumption, and nativity.

VIII. Conception is that by which, by a singular operation of the Holy Spirit, it began to exist in the womb of the virgin Mary from her own seed. This is taught in Genesis 3:15; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:18,20; Luke 1:30-31 — and indeed supernaturally and by the immediate power of the Holy Spirit, in respect of which He is singularly called not begotten but made (Romans 1:3; Galatians 4:4), and holy (Luke 1:34-35; Hebrews 7:26), and is compared with the first Adam not as to the matter of the body but as to the mode of conception (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45,47).

IX. The assumption of human nature by the Word is that by which the Son of God, at the very first moment of conception, bestowed His own personality on that human substance in Marys womb that was properly without subsistence or personality. For Leo the Great rightly says (epistle XI): Our nature was not so assumed that it was first created and afterward assumed, but that it was created by the very assumption — lest anyone suppose the humanity existed before it was united to the Word. Compare Hebrews 2:16; Colossians 2:9; Philippians 2:7.

X. Nativity is that by which the Son of God was brought forth into the light as a true human from the virgin Mary at the mature and lawful time of birth. From the prediction of Moses (Genesis 49:10) and of Isaiah 7:14; Micah 5:2; Luke 2:6-7,22-23 teaches Christs birth, as also Paul in Galatians 4:4.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): IX. — 1 Corinthians 15:45,47). — Hebrews 7:26), and stands as compared with ye first Adam not as to ye matter belonging toward ye body but as to ye mode belonging toward conception (Romans 5:14; — Galatians 4:4), and holy (Luke 1:34-35; — Luke 1:30-31 — and indeed supernaturally and by ye immediate power belonging toward ye Holy Spirit, in respect belonging toward which He stands as singularly called not begotten but made (Romans 1:3; — Matthew 1:18,20; — Isaiah 7:14; — This stands as taught in Genesis 3:15; — Conception stands as that by which, by a singular operation belonging toward ye Holy Spirit, it began to exist in ye womb belonging toward ye virgin Mary out from her own seed. — VIII. — Further, belonging toward ye human nature stand as considered conception, assumption, and nativity. — VII.

title: XI–XIII. Personal union; ineffable mode neither essential nor accidental
latin: XI. Unio personalis est, qua Filius Dei naturam assumptam sibi in personae suae unitatem coniunxit. XII. In ea spectatur modus & effectus. XIII. Modus quamvis ineffabilis sit, tamen negatur esse coniunctionem sive unionem eamque neque essentialem, qua quae mutuum & naturalem respectum habent ad se invicem uniuntur, ut actus & potentia, materia & forma, genus & differentia specifica; neque accidentalem, qua vel subiectis accidentia, vel ipsa substantia inter se accidentaliter coniunguntur: sed personalem, qua in personalitate Verbi tanquam communi vinculo naturae distinctae, & nulla naturali inclinatione ad unionem propendentes, in unum colligantur, cuius unionis similis alia non invenitur in universa rerum natura — contra Eutychen naturas confundentem & Nestorium eas distrahentem & unitatem personae Christi perperam dissolventem. Quoniam igitur una utriusque naturae est personalitas, idcirco & una est persona & personalis unio, argumento 1 Cor. 8:6; Ioh. 20:31; 1 Ioh. 4:15; Ioh. 9:37.
english: XI. Personal union is that by which the Son of God joined the assumed nature to Himself into the unity of His person. XII. In it are contemplated mode and effect.

XIII. Although the mode is ineffable, it is denied to be a conjunction or union that is either essential — by which things having a mutual and natural respect to one another are united, as act and potency, matter and form, genus and specific difference — or accidental, by which either accidents are joined to subjects or substances themselves are accidentally joined among themselves: but personal, by which in the personality of the Word as a common bond distinct natures, not inclining by any natural tendency to union, are gathered into one — a union whose like is not found in the whole nature of things — against Eutyches confusing the natures and Nestorius tearing them apart and wrongly dissolving the unity of Christs person.
Since therefore there is one personality of both natures, there is also one person and one personal union (1 Corinthians 8:6; John 20:31; 1 John 4:15; John 9:37).
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): John 9:37). — 1 John 4:15; — John 20:31; — Since therefore there stands as one personality belonging toward both natures, there stands as also one person and one personal union (1 Corinthians 8:6; — but personal, by which in ye personality belonging toward ye Word as a common bond distinct natures, not inclining by any natural tendency to union, stand as gathered into one — a union whose like stands as not found in ye whole nature belonging toward things — against Eutyches confusing ye natures and Nestorius tearing them apart and wrongly dissolving ye unity belonging toward Christs person. — Although ye mode stands as ineffable, it stands as denied to be a conjunction or union that stands as either essential — by which things having a mutual and natural respect to one another stand as united, as act and potency, matter and form, genus and specific difference — or accidental, by which either accidents stand as joined to subjects or substances themselves stand as accidentally joined among themselves: — XIII. — In it stand as contemplated mode and effect. — XII. — Personal union stands as that by which ye Son belonging toward God joined ye assumed nature to Himself into ye unity belonging toward His person. — XI.

title: XIV. Effect of the union: communion of natures and communication of idioms; Cap.2 close toward Cap.3
latin: XIV. Effectus unionis personalis est communio tum naturarum, tum proprietatum, quae dicitur communicatio idiomatum. Propter quam de se invicem praedicantur, non quidem absolute & abstracte, sed per vocabula concreta quae involvunt suppositum, & connotant personalitatem, in qua naturae conveniunt. Nam ratio, propter quam una natura de altera praedicatur, nulla est alia, quam unio hypostatica in eodem supposito. Quapropter nefas est dicere absolute Deum esse passum, aut hominem creasse caelum; sed per concreta recte unum de altero, & proprietas atque operatio alterius de altero enunciabitur, ut Deus est homo, homo est Deus, Deus est passus & mortuus, homo est aeternus, condidit caelum & terram. Damascenus appellat antidosis onomaton, & Melanchthon finit praedicationem, in qua proprietas uni naturae conveniens tribuitur personae in concreto. Ut enim unitas personae & unio personalis, ita & duarum naturarum in Christo distinctio necessario retinetur. Quia vero personae per vocabula concreta significatae utriusque naturae idiomata indifferenter tribuuntur, idcirco propter discrimen naturarum, ut sciatur secundum utram naturam praedicatum subiecto conveniat, addi id ipsum nonnunquam solet. CAPUT TERTIUM sequitur, De officiis Iesu Christi.
english: XIV. The effect of the personal union is the communion both of the natures and of the properties, which is called the communication of idioms. On account of it they are predicated of one another — not absolutely and abstractly, but through concrete words that involve the supposit and connote the personality in which the natures agree. For the reason why one nature is predicated of the other is none other than the hypostatic union in the same supposit.

Therefore it is unlawful to say absolutely that God suffered, or that a human created heaven; but through concretes one is rightly declared of the other, and the property and operation of the one of the other — as God is human, the human is God, God suffered and died, the human is eternal and made heaven and earth. Damascene calls this an exchange of names, and Melanchthon defines the predication in which a property belonging to one nature is attributed to the person in the concrete. For just as the unity of person and the personal union, so also the distinction of the two natures in Christ is necessarily retained. And because the idioms of both natures are attributed indifferently to the person signified by concrete words, therefore on account of the difference of natures it is sometimes usual to add according to which nature the predicate belongs to the subject.
CHAPTER THREE follows, On the offices of Jesus Christ.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): CHAPTER THREE follows, On ye offices belonging toward Jesus Christ. — And because ye idioms belonging toward both natures stand as attributed indifferently to ye person signified by concrete words, therefore on account belonging toward ye difference belonging toward natures it stands as sometimes usual to add according to which nature ye predicate belongs to ye subject. — For just as ye unity belonging toward person and ye personal union, so also ye distinction belonging toward ye two natures in Christ stands as necessarily retained. — Damascene calls this an exchange belonging toward names, and Melanchthon defines ye predication in which a property belonging to one nature stands as attributed to ye person in ye concrete. — but through concretes one stands as rightly declared belonging toward ye other, and ye property and operation belonging toward ye one belonging toward ye other — as God stands as human, ye human stands as God, God suffered and died, ye human stands as eternal and made heaven and earth. — Therefore it stands as unlawful to say absolutely that God suffered, or that a human created heaven; — For ye reason why one nature stands as predicated belonging toward ye other stands as none other than ye hypostatic union in ye same supposit. — On account belonging toward it they stand as predicated belonging toward one another — not absolutely and abstractly, but through concrete words that involve ye supposit and connote ye personality in which ye natures agree. — The effect belonging toward ye personal union stands as ye communion both belonging toward ye natures and belonging toward ye properties, which stands as called ye communication belonging toward idioms. — XIV.
